scenes.label: The vocabulary of a sealed test
scenes.text: Let us slow down and name these words. You know, in-sample is the part we use to choose. Out-of-sample is the part we save for later. The first part gives us a way to build the rule, and the second part lets us see what happens with new prices. Overfitting is when the rule follows the old path too closely. Curve-fitting is the same problem when we move the settings. If you try enough settings, you will find something that looks good, but that does not mean it will work again. Frozen parameters are the numbers we leave alone. A segmented backtest has fixed blocks with separate jobs. Walk-forward moves the start and does it again. In this run, we have one first part and one later part. That gives us context; this run has no walk-forward result. Warmup bars are the history an indicator needs before we use its value. We keep them outside the trade-result count. That is a method rule; it adds no new SPY result.

scenes.label: Why selection pressure matters
scenes.text: Why does this matter? You know, the problem starts when the development history feels too familiar. You look at the old prices, try many rules, and keep the one that looks good. Then you start to learn the path instead of testing the idea. Curve-fitting can mean moving one threshold, one exit, or one window after you see the result. White's data-snooping paper warns that a result can show up by chance when the same data chooses and judges the rule. Trading-rule research gives us the same warning. The simple answer is to choose the plan first. Freeze the settings. Open the later block once. Record what happened. SPY shows the first stop. Dow shows why the later step matters.
scenes.speaker_directions: Calm, precise beginner teaching; pause after exact numbers and before the boundary.

scenes.text: Now look at the group along with the one candidate. A distribution is the group of results. It has a center, a spread, and a shape. scenes.label: Fixed blocks are not walk-forward
scenes.text: Segmentation and walk-forward sound alike, so keep them apart. You know, one version uses fixed blocks, and each block has a job; a segmented backtest does that. Walk-forward moves the start and does it again through time. Choose the design from the question, the history, and the update rule. Research on data over time says order matters, and conditions can change. In this run, we have one SPY intake and no later phase. We have one Dow later block. That is the full set of blocks here. It does not make the run walk-forward. A rolling test needs dates and a rule for when to update or leave the settings alone.

scenes.text: Here is the worksheet. Write down the instrument, the timeframe, and the rule; then write the first window, the later window, the counts, and the validation. Put the units next to each comparison. For SPY, write five in, zero survive, zero forward, and holdout not reached. For Dow, write 184 in, 154 survive, and 30 drop; one candidate changes from positive net profit to negative. Freeze first. Save the source hash and the row location. Name the later window before you call it out-of-sample. Pin the group before you use a median or percentile. That turns a chart into a question you can repeat.
